title.en: Dilingavuv and the Pit of Roasted Chestnuts
title.zh: 迪林加武武與烤栗陷阱

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖托雷斯群島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Dilingavuv ate his neighbours' bananas from the treetops; no one dared his bat-like stretched arms until Marawhihi shot off his ear. The thief cut himself a new ear from a Raw root, lured the celebrating dancers one by one onto a leaf-cloak over a pit, and rained hot stones in — but Marawhihi shot an arrow-chain up a banyan branch and led them all out alive.
summary.zh: 迪林加武武天天攀上香蕉樹偷食，村人畏其張臂如蝠，無人敢近；唯最機敏的馬拉威希希以卡薩林木箭射落其耳。迪林加武武回家瞞母索斧，自砍 Raw 樹根另造一耳，口中念『剁碎！剁開！』；村人偷聽而知。馬拉威希希率眾日日宴舞，迪林加武武欲報仇：他備下烤栗、火石與葉衣，在村旁掘深坑覆以葉衣，誘歇腳的舞者一一坐上而陷落，馬拉威希希最後也跌入。他把燒紅的石頭擲進坑裡；馬拉威希希卻叫眾人移到坑的另一邊避過。他抬頭見坑口懸著一根榕枝，便連環射箭成梯，眾人攀箭而出，皆得生還。

passages.text: They were living in their place, and his companions made a garden, and planted bananas in it. When the bananas bore fruit and ripened Dilingavuv went every day and ate bananas in their garden, not eating on the ground, but climbing into the trees and eating. After a while he was discovered; one of the party went into the garden and saw him up in a banana-tree eating; so he ran and told the others. Says he, 'You fellows, I have seen the one who steals and eats our bananas.' Then said Marawhihi, 'Hew out bows for us to go and shoot and kill him.' But they said, 'Marawhihi, no one will be able to shoot and kill him. It is wholly impossible.' However they hewed out bows, each for himself, and put points to their arrows; and when that was done Marawhihi said, 'Let us go after him one by one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So one went first, and came to the garden, and saw him sitting up in the banana-tree, and went on tiptoe towards him to shoot him. But Dilingavuv stretched out his arms like a bat, and the man was afraid, and ran back and told the others. Thus they all went in turn, and came back and disputed with Marawhihi, saying, 'It can't possibly be done.' Then said Marawhihi, 'I shall do it myself, I shall shoot him and kill him.' And this Marawhihi they say was more clever than them all; and he went last and saw Dilingavuv sitting in the banana-tree, and he stepped along on tiptoe under the banana, and when Dilingavuv stretched out his arms he was not frightened at him; but he shot him with a bird arrow of casuarina wood, and hit him on the ear, and shot it right off; and he fell headlong to the ground. So Marawhihi ran and told his friends; but Dilingavuv got up from under the banana and went home to his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he reached his mother's house, he called to her within, and she answered him and said, 'What is it, my son?' And he said, 'Give me an axe.' But he deceived her, and did not tell her that Marawhihi had shot his ear off. Then he went and cut another ear for himself out of the root of a tree, and the name of that tree is the Raw, and as he was chopping the Raw root, he said, 'Chop in pieces! chop asunder!' But Marawhihi had sent one of his men who went and listened, and heard him saying this, and he ran back and told Marawhihi that Dilingavuv was chopping himself out an ear in place of the other. After this Marawhihi and his men made a feast and danced, and danced every day. And when Dilingavuv heard of it, he said, 'I will go and have my revenge.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So he gathered a great quantity of Tahitian chestnuts, and took fire, and collected stones, and took a dancing cloak of leaves, and went to them; but he did not go right up to them into the open, but stayed beside the village. Then he made up a fire and roasted his chestnuts, and heated the stones, and dug a very deep hole and covered over the mouth of it with the dress of leaves; and so he sat and watched them dancing. Before long one of them fell out to take breath; and when he saw Dilingavuv sitting and eating chestnuts, he called to him to give him one. 'Run over here,' says Dilingavuv; so he runs over to him, and sits down on this dancing dress; and as he throws himself down to sit he goes clean down into the hole. And Dilingavuv played the same trick to all the company at that dance, and let them all down into that one pit, and Marawhihi last of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Made a Friend of an Eel

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A boy begged two yams of his parents, and the crumbs he dropped called up an eel that turned into a man. They anointed their heads and dug gardens together, till the jealous villagers fell on him; a flood carried the eel to the beach, where they cut him to pieces — but his brother's tears revived him, and he sent the family to another island before a great surf swept the persecutors' island wholly away.
summary.zh: 一童求父母留兩隻芋，烤食時碎屑落入水中，一條鰻來食，化為男子。二人抹油束髮，同去園中掘地；村人圍觀，婦女怠工，丈夫們怒而毆鰻；童以水澆之，鰻復原形，屢擒屢脫，躍入水中。村人言『放雨淹他』，遂作大雨，洪水把鰻沖上灘頭，眾人將鰻剁成數段。童之弟奔下灘，見而哭泣；淚落鰻身，鰻復化為人，起身對弟說：『你回去告訴父母，我們三人要遷往別島。』三人遷走後，某日一老嫗聽見鰻歌聲，村人初不信；聲音分明，歌罷忽有巨響，滔天巨浪席捲全村，無一倖存，全島盡沒。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Vanua Lava heritage.

passages.text: They were living in their place, and they were planting their gardens; and one day when they went to plant, a boy said to his father and mother, 'To-morrow when you go again, you will put by a yam for me.' Next morning his father and mother went, and put by a yam for him; and he roasted it and ate it, and then went and asked some other boys for more. But they scolded him; and he cried and said, 'Very well!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning they put two yams for the boy; and when he had roasted them he went and followed a stream, and found a nice place, and sat down to eat. As he was eating, crumbs of food fell into the water, and an Eel came out and ate, and turned into a man, and rose up and came to the boy. When they two had eaten all the yam, the Eel said to the boy, 'To-morrow you will roast two yams again, and bring them here, and we two will eat them.' And when they had finished eating the Eel said to the boy, 'Let us anoint our heads.' So they dressed their heads and adorned themselves, and went into the garden, and helped the people who were digging the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they had finished eating the Eel said to the boy, 'Let us anoint our heads.' So they dressed their heads and adorned themselves, and went into the garden, and helped the people who were digging the ground. But when that Eel dug the ground all the people crowded to see him do it; some went back to their digging, but the women would not do their work, and their husbands were exceedingly angry with the Eel, and rushed upon him, and would have killed him; but the boy who came with him poured water on him, and he turned into an Eel again. And they caught hold of him, but he escaped; and they missed their hold upon him over and over again, and he jumped into the water. So they said, 'All right, we will make rain for him'; and they made a great rain, and the water swelled into a flood and carried the Eel to the beach. When the flood subsided they went down and found the Eel lying on the beach, and they cut him into short pieces, and left him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the boy, his brother, ran down and saw the Eel lying there, and wept; and his tears fell upon the Eel, and he turned into a man again, and stood up and said to his brother, 'You are to go up inland and tell your father and mother that you three are to go and take up your abode in another island.' The boy therefore said to his father and mother, 'We three are to move to another island.' After they had gone, one day an old woman was sitting, and she heard the Eel singing a song; and she said to the people, 'Listen to that singing a song like the Eel'; but some of them answered, 'It is not that, the Eel is dead'; but they heard plainly the Eel's voice, and said, 'It is true, it is the Eel's voice.' And when he had finished singing they heard a loud report; and as they were sitting a very great surf rose and swept them away, all of them; and they all died, and that island was entirely lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: Molgon and Molwor: The Brothers Whose Names Told Their Fate
title.zh: 莫爾貢與莫爾沃：名讖成真

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Orphaned Molgon was told to feed his little brother; but paddling up a stream after the galakv fruit that floated past, he left Molwor in the canoe and stayed with a woman named Rohehahal — who read out their names like a judgement: 'Your name is Molgon, Go-catch, and you have caught on to the goods of you and me; but he, his name is Molwor, Go-clear, and he has come here to be clear of all the goods of you and me.' Molwor lay dead in the sun; Molgon's tears revived him; and the brother's last song ended in the water, where blood rose up and both turned into stones in the water-course.
summary.zh: 父母臨終囑長兄莫爾貢照看幼弟莫爾沃。二人划舟溯流，見 galakv 果一枚枚漂來，數目漸增；至果源處，兄留弟守舟，獨自上岸採果。婦人 Rohehahal 自屋出，與他共炊共食；他吃不完便想帶給弟弟，婦人卻說『吃不完就丟給豬』。他哭。她問名，聞言道：『果然！你名莫爾貢（Go-catch），你已捉住了你我之家的財物；他那名莫爾沃（Go-clear），是來躲開你我全部家產的。』兄弟返舟見幼弟已被烈日曬死；莫爾貢淚滴弟胸，弟復活，責兄只顧自食。婦人屢催兄『跟我走』；弟唱罷離歌，雙足入水化鰻，一躍而沒，兄亦躍水；婦人立崖下望，只見水中泛起血光——二人化為溪中兩塊臥石。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Vanua Lava heritage.

passages.text: The father and mother of these two brothers, who lived at Gaua, said to the elder of them, Molgon, 'You are to look well after him, the younger one, and feed him well.' 'All right,' he said; and then their father and mother died. They two lived on; and one day they drew down a canoe, and paddled up the course of a stream, and came upon galakv fruit floating down it. They broke it in two and ate it. They paddled on and there came floating down two, then three, then four, then five, then six, then seven, then eight, then nine, then ten, one for one and one for the other, and the odd one they broke in two; they paddled on and saw the source from which the fruits had floated down. Then the elder brother said to the younger, 'You sit here, and I will go and gather for us both to eat.' So he went and gathered fruit. But a woman, Rohehahal, came out of her house, and looked down to where he was standing, and called him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went to her, and she said to him, 'We two will cook food in the oven'; and they two cooked food in the oven, and afterwards they ate. He could not eat all the qeta, and he said to her, 'I will go with this to my brother, that he may eat it'; but the woman said, 'If you can't eat it all, throw it outside for the pigs'; and he cried. Then she made a mush; he could not eat it all, and said, 'I shall take this for my brother to eat.' But she said, 'Throw it outside to the pigs'; and he cried. Then she asked their names, and said, 'Aia! true enough! your name is Molgon, Go-catch, and you have caught on to the pigs which belong to you and me, and the house, and the gamal, and the food, and the money; but he, his name is Molwor, Go-clear, and he has come here to be clear of all the goods of you and me.' And he cried and cried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the woman said, 'Get up, let us go and see him'; and they went over and found him dead, lying in the canoe, for the sun had smitten him dead with its rays. And he cried and cried, and his tears dropped on his brother's breast, and he came to life again, and said, 'Brother, our father when he died told you to take care of me, but you have gone away to eat and have not thought of me.' But the woman urged Molgon, 'Come here! we two will go up away from him again.' Then Molwor sang a song to him, and got down from the canoe, and put his legs into the water, and began to turn into an eel; and when he had quite finished his song he plunged into the water, and his brother leapt down also into the water. And the woman stood and looked down, and blood came up from the water. And they two turned into stones lying in the water-course; and the woman stood and wept greatly, and went back again up the hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: In famine, a son tracked his mother's secret gaviga-tree and met the ghost who owned it — his own uncle, who hid him from the whirring ghost-flock and fed him till daylight, then gave him a damsel for a wife. Her touch ripened every garden; her husband called her a sky-woman and beat her, and she burned banyan leaves and rose in the smoke to her own country, the child crying beside the fire — until Marawa the Spider spun a line to heaven, carried father and child up, and at the feast each pass of the dancing mother drew the cry 'Mother!' until she stopped, knew her own, and came home with them all.
summary.zh: 饑荒年，母子靠母親偷采的 gaviga 果度日；兒子發現果核追問，循母親折枝記號至果樹，夜攀樹而食。一個鬼落在他身旁，自認是他的舅舅，把他藏進樹洞，蓋住洞口；群鬼嗡嗡而至采果，舅舅摘果分他，直吃到天亮。臨散時，舅舅將一個少女許配給他。女子觸物皆熟：摸薯即得薯，摸香蕉即熟蕉，摸椰即得椰。丈夫見狀疑心，責打她，罵她屬天不屬地。她說『好，我就回天上去』，便燒起榕葉，火焰直上，她從煙中升天，孩子啼哭於火旁。丈夫求助於蜘蛛馬拉瓦；馬拉瓦吐絲成線直通天庭，背負父子而上。天庭正開盛宴，母子每相錯而過，孩子便哭喊一聲『媽媽！』；她終於停步，問『是誰在喊我媽媽？』認出孩子與丈夫，便隨蜘蛛攜全家平安回到地上。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); the ending comes from Codrington's summary of the continuation. Mota heritage.

passages.text: They were living and living in their place; a famine prevailed. And there was a woman and her son, and they both were hungry. After a time the mother went to dig qauro, wild yams, for them to eat, and as she went she found a gaviga (Malay apple) tree in fruit, in a deserted garden, and she put down her basket, and gathered with her hands and ate. And when she had finished eating she put some seeds into her basket; and as she went along she broke the tips of the branches to mark the path. And when she had arrived at the village she said to her son, 'Take the things out of our basket'; and he took them out one by one, and as he took them out he found the gaviga seeds in the basket which his mother had put there. Then says her son to her, 'What is this you have been eating, and have put the seeds in the basket for me to see?' But he says, 'No!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: So he follows the word his mother gave him; and as he goes along the sun is setting, but he arrives at the gaviga-tree and climbs up. And when he had climbed up to eat it was dark. Then he sees something flying to him on the gaviga and settling. 'Where do you come from?' says the ghost. And the man tells him of his mother and her gaviga. Then said the ghost, 'She is my sister to be sure, and my own nephew are you; come here and let me hide you, for we are many of us now coming to eat gavigas.' So he makes him sit down in the hollow of the gaviga, and sits over the mouth of it. While he is in the hollow he hears a whirring sound like birds settling on the top of the tree. 'What is this?' says the man. 'Ghosts come to eat gavigas; don't be afraid, here am I with you,' says the uncle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when the day was dawning and some of the ghosts were taking flight he says to a damsel among them, 'Don't be in a hurry to fly off, you and I will fly together'; and she says, 'Very well.' But when they had all the lot of them taken flight, and it was clear daylight, the ghost says to the man, 'Well now, come out'; and he comes out from the hollow of the gaviga-tree. Then says the ghost his uncle to him, 'Well, here is a damsel for a qorolava [wife].'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: So he married her. She takes her child up on her back, and goes with it to the yam garden; if she lays hold on the leaf of the yam, there is a tuber already in her hand; if she essays to pluck hibiscus leaves, they are in her hand already; and if she essays to take a cocoa-nut, there is a cocoa-nut already in her hand. But her husband will not believe her: 'You don't belong down here below, you belong above the sky. Get back into your own country.' And she says, 'Very well, I will soon go back into my own country.' So she gathers banyan leaves into a heap, and sets fire to them, and the smoke goes straight up into the clouds, and the child's mother goes up in it; and her child cries beside the fire, and she goes on up into the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript and Codrington's summary of the continuation; not verbatim.

title.en: Ganviviris and Ro Som, the Woman Called Money
title.zh: 加維維里斯與『錢』女羅松

region.en: Uakea, Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島烏阿凱阿（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Ganviviris, an idle orphan kept poor by his uncle, shot at a rolling sauma at a voice's urging and was dragged by the fish into the cave of Ro Som — Money — who turned from fish to woman and promised him service. Ten plaited bags filled with coin in the night; he bought wives, taro-gardens, pigs, and rank after rank of the Suqe to the top. But at the height of his kolikole feast a woman with boar's tusks on her arms walked up the slope and into his house; his bags stood empty, his pigs were gone, and in five days he was dead.
summary.zh: 加維維里斯是孤兒，寄居舅家，舅母們譏他游手好閒、無產無份。一日他下灘射魚，正要放箭，忽聞身後有人催喝『放箭！放箭！』回頭無人；第三次放箭果中一條游動的 sauma 大魚；魚負他竄入乾洞——那正是羅松（意為『錢』）的住處。魚化為女子，說：『莫哭，是我在憐憫你。我天天看你，如今要幫你了。』她教他請舅母編十只袋子，掛滿屋中。夜裡屋梁被錢壓得吱呀作響——十袋皆滿。他以此娶妻、買園、養豬、一級級買進蘇蓋會社，直到最高之位。大宴 kolikole 之夕，見一女子拄矛拾級而上，臂戴鐲與野豬牙，髮插豬尾；她徑入加維維里斯屋中，轉眼不見。他上屋查看，十袋皆空，豬隻全無；分發出去的財物盡作廢。當夜他喊叫不安，自此病倒，第五日死去。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); records the Suqe rank-system economy in narrative form.

passages.text: The story about what Ro Som did for Ganviviris is not an old one; he was a man whom my father's grandfather and his friends had seen; an orphan, whose father and mother were both dead, he lived with his mother's brother. And his uncle did nothing for him in the suqe club; he still remained an arlava, because he was an idle fellow, and when they were all gone inland to the gardens he would go down to the beach to shoot fish, and do nothing else day after day. But one day he took his bow and went down to Ngerenow, and there he saw a sauma slowly swimming along and rolling from side to side quite close to him; and he took an arrow tipped with casuarina wood, and drew his bow to shoot. And just as he was releasing the string he heard a voice inciting him and saying, 'Let fly! Let fly!' And he turned his head again and again to look behind him, but there was no man. And the third time he drew his bow, and heard the voice, and loosed the string and hit the sauma.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he ran down and caught the fish by the tail, and threw his arms round it; but the fish struggled, and carried him off into a dry cave, which was, they say, the dwelling of Ro Som (Money). And Ganviviris cried aloud, but the sauma turned into a woman, and said, 'Don't cry, it is I who have had pity on you. I have seen you every day, and now I am going to do you a service. Tell your uncle to bid his wives plait bags for you, and let them be ten, and make a chamber for yourself parted off from the house, and hang up all the bags in the open; and don't eat anything to-day.' So Ganviviris dived out of the cave, and went back into the village, and got the three wives to plait the bags. And in the night Ro Som came and said, 'Make haste to hang up your bags.' And next day he hung up the bags; and in the night he heard the rafters creak because of the money which was filling the bags; and he felt one after another those ten bags, every one quite full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Ro Som said to him, 'Tell your uncle to give you his third wife'; and his uncle let him have one. And always he was buying food with large payments, and he paddled over to Vanua Lava and bought with large sums there, and to Mota and bought with large sums there: and he went on in the suqe till he reached the wemeleloa. Then he desired to make his suqe also at Mota, and he went and built his house at Tasmate; and he appointed the tenth day for a sawae, and at the sawae the tenth day for a kolekole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And at the kolekole, when the noise of the sawae was sounding like thunder, and the feast was at its height, they saw a woman walking up the sloping ground below the cliff, using a spear for a walking stick, with bracelets on her arms reaching to the elbow, and on her right arm a boar's tusk, and her head smeared with red earth, and pigs' tails fastened to her hair; and they thought that some visitors had just landed from a canoe. And she went straight to the house of Ganviviris and passed out of sight within it. And they told Ganviviris, 'We have seen a woman go into your hole house, with bracelets and boars' tusks on her arms'; and he said, 'Don't mention it in the village.' And he went up there to bring out his money-bags on his back, and he saw that his ten bags had nothing in them; and he went outside and saw that all his pigs were gone; his distribution of property came to nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Orphan Whose Mother Was Money

region.en: Mota and Sanwawa landing, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島三瓦瓦灘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Scorned by the 'children of fathers' — 'you have no father, you have no mother, who will give you food to eat with your fish?' — the Little Orphan fished alone at Sanwawa, and out of the sea on his line came fish, a plaited hibiscus line, and at last a woman and her child: Ro Som, Money, and her child. She gave him house, gamal, endless cooked food, sprouting gardens, and pigs with curled tusks; he ate his way to the top of every rank of the Suqe, repaying his uncle's every payment. But when he scolded her without cause on his return from Gaua, Ro Som wept till sundown, then slipped away by night with her child, heavy with the money-bags — and the village was a deserted garden by morning.
summary.zh: 『有父之子女』譏小孤兒：『你無父無母，誰給你備菜配魚？』他獨自到三瓦瓦灘垂釣，魚、編織的扶桑繩一一上鉤，最後竟從海裡上來一個女人帶著孩子——羅松（錢）母子。她說『我們三個一起走吧』，給他蓋了房與男子會所，備下吃不完的熟食，園中香蕉、芋頭自行抽芽，豬有卷牙的公豬與母豬成群。他一級級買進蘇蓋，直到頂級，舅父的每一次付出他都以錢與豬如數奉還。後隨船赴高阿島，無豬可送，只帶一枚未開的蛤；歸來見食物未動，疑母親另有野男人供養，出言羞辱。羅松與孩子哭到日落；待他睡熟，悄悄卸開錢袋負重而逃，一袋墜地，一頭卷牙豬仍縛在三瓦瓦灘。天明孤兒醒來，村中已是一片荒園。老嫗唱歌相告：『看那邊！兩個又從他釣起她們的海裡下去了。』

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Mota heritage.

passages.text: They were living in their place, the boys were growing up, and their father and mother said to them, 'Go down to the beach, and catch fish with hook and line for us, and we two will go inland and get vegetables for us all to eat with them.' And as they were going along the path the Little Orphan said, 'Let me go with you.' But they said, 'E-o-o! not you, a little orphan, we will go by ourselves alone, we who are children of fathers; if you were to go with us what would you eat? You have no father, you have no mother, who will give you food to eat with your fish?' And the children of fathers went down to the beach, and the Little Orphan went down a steep place eastwards to the landing-place at Sanwawa; and there he fishes for himself with a line and hook.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And as he stood down there, a fish comes on his hook first; and then a nipanau; and a nongpitpit; and a gavaru; and then a plaited hibiscus line; and then a woman and her child come up out of the sea to him; and their name is Ro Som (Money), and he puts them down on the reef. Then Ro Som says to him, 'Let us three go together.' But he says, 'Not you two; I will go by myself, because I have no food to feed you with.' But she says, 'Never mind, string our fish together and we three will go.' So the three went along and arrived at the Little Orphan's dwelling-place; and he sees a house and a gamal; and he asks, 'Whose house is this?' And Ro Som says, 'It is the house of us three, and your gamal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Ro Som says to the Little Orphan, 'Come now, cook the fish for us three to eat.' But he says, 'What are we going to eat the fish with? I told you that you two must not come with me; I have no food.' But she says, 'Cook the fish, we three will eat them with some vegetable food presently.' So he makes up a fire for the fish, and they three sit down and wait. Then Ro Som says to him, 'Now then, take down our fish.' And she says, 'Look, there is a heap of cooked food there for us to eat the fish with.' So he goes over to the fish, and takes them off the fire, and they three ate. And when they had finished eating he goes out of the house into the village and sees gardens, a banana garden, and a tomago garden, and a yam garden, a wowosa garden, a reawea garden, a sugar-cane garden; and the bananas were beginning to rot, and the tomatoes were sprouting afresh, and the yams were sprouting. And Ro Som says to him, 'They belong to us three only.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Ro Som says, 'To-morrow you will make up fires in the gamal in every oven, and we two will be here in the house, and we three will make mixture of cooked food and scraped cocoa-nut for food for pigs.' And as soon as they covered in the ovens the food was cooked; the pigs' food made by the two in the house was a hundred baskets-full, and that in the gamal a hundred. And Ro Som says, 'Well now, call the pigs, sumsum'; and he hears continued squealing, and he sees boars with tusks that curl and meet, and rawe, and sows; these all come rushing out to the three, and the three feed them and they eat. And while they are eating, Ro Som says to him, 'Have you got any uncle on your mother's side? Run and say to him, Tata, come and make the payments for my steps in the tuqe.' So his uncle paid rank after rank, and his nephew brought money out on his back, and gave pigs and rawes, and made return of his uncle's property.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Orphan's Voyage, and the Empty Village
title.zh: 小孤兒航海歸、村成荒園

region.en: Gaua and Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島高阿島與莫塔島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: When the Motalava and Losalava people paddled over to Gaua, the Little Orphan went too — with no pig, only an unopened cockle-shell in his hand. On Gaua every man ran down crying 'This is my friend!' to every other; nobody wanted to be friends with the orphan. He came home and scolded Ro Som for the food they had not eaten, and she and her child wept till sundown; then while he slept they ran away with the money-bags, and the village became a deserted garden, one bag fallen by the path and a tusked pig still tied at Sanwawa.
summary.zh: 莫塔拉瓦與洛薩拉瓦人划舟赴高阿島，小孤兒也去；別人皆帶豬，他只帶一枚未開的蛤貝。抵岸時，村人一個個跑下灘喊『這是我的朋友！』與各自的友人攜手上岸；唯獨沒人要與孤兒結交。風起返航，他搶先跑回家中，見那堆食物原封未動，便疑心母親另有男人供野食給她們，出言相責。羅松母子哭到日落；孤兒靠近她們，躺在他們腿上哄勸不成，自己竟先睡去。她們輕輕抽腿放下他的頭，奔向錢袋，解開豬繩，背負而逃。她們一出村，村子立時變成荒蕪的園地。行至三瓦瓦灘，老嫗負袋吃力，一袋墜地；一頭插著卷牙的豬仍拴在那裡。孤兒醒來追尋，直至海邊，老嫗唱道：『看那邊！Iolo! Ialo! 兩個正從他釣起她們之處重新沉入海裡。』

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Mota heritage. Second half of the Little Orphan cycle.

passages.text: And the Little Orphan goes into the house, and makes a fire, and puts pig's flesh into the oven to make it keep. And when he has finished with his pig, then comes a report of a voyage, that the Motalava people with the Losalava people are going to paddle over to Gaua. Then says the Little Orphan to his mother, 'Oh, mother, those people are going to paddle over to Gaua to-morrow, and may I?' And his mother says, 'You must not: stay and look after your meat in the oven.' But he says, 'E-o-o! not so, mother, I shall go on the voyage with them; I am going to them, and you two will cook my pig for me.' So it was night and morning; and when morning was come he goes up inside the house and speaks to his mother and says, 'Well, mother, as I am going away from you two, and you two stay here, there is that heap of food you are to eat; but these you are not to touch.' And he goes off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when he reaches the landing-place, he sees that those people have already dragged down the canoe and set it afloat on the edge of the sea; and he runs and jumps up and climbs right up on board the canoe, and they paddle off. But they all of them had taken pigs with them, but the Little Orphan had not taken one for himself, and he had brought nothing but a cockle-shell in his hand, and that shell-fish was not opened. And when they brought the canoes to shore at Gaua, the people there came down to meet them, and one of them runs over and cries, 'Friend!' and touches his friend's hand, and the two go up the beach together; and some other runs down and cries, 'This is my friend'; and some other runs down and cries, 'This is my friend,' and takes him; but that poor Little Orphan, they don't want to be friends with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when those people drag up their canoe at Mota, he runs back, runs and runs, and reaches the house where they three lived, and sees the heap of yams still remaining as it was; and he says, 'What have you two been eating? this food still remains untouched.' But he says, 'No, there is some other man I think has been bringing you wild food of the forest.' Now he makes a fool of himself in this, supposing that it was as if his mother were living with a man. But that female Ro Som wept exceedingly because he had been angry with her, and she and her child wept till the sun went down; and they cried on, till they heard the nose of the Little Orphan whistling in sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they removed softly their legs, and put down his head on the ground; and they run to the money-bags, and unloose the pig, and the two run off. And as they went out that village turned into a deserted garden. But as they ran away the old woman sat down, the bags of money were very heavy upon her, and one of the bags fell down. And a pig with tusks remained tied at that landing-place at Sanwawa, and that money-bag remained lying where it fell. And that Little Orphan woke and jumped up, and there he was in a deserted garden, and he ran looking for those two, and he came out upon the shore, and sees an old woman sitting there and asks, 'Oh! have you seen anybody at all here just now?' And she sings, 'Look, look over there! Iolo! Ialo! the two are plunging back into the sea at the place where the Little Orphan had fished them up.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: Wowut-ta-Taragariga and the Orphan Who Fed the Dead Man's Feast

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded (native MS, summarized) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX note

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX, concluding note on two Mota stories

summary.en: Wowut-ta-Taragariga's parents kept him in the house till he was grown, then advanced him at once to the highest Suqe rank; no one dared approach his gamal but an orphan, who carried him a portion of another man's feast. Wowut took a liking to the orphan and paid him money; the boy came again and again with food till he had 'thousands of money, thousands of boars, thousands of pigs with curled tusks,' and rose himself to high rank. When Wowut died he directed that when his friend came to mourn over him he was to be given his wife in memory of him.
summary.zh: 沃武特·塔·塔拉加里加自幼被父母關在家中，直至成年，方一舉晉入蘇蓋最高之級；他的會所令人生畏，無人敢近，唯有一名孤兒受託替另一家把宴席的一份送進去。沃武特喜歡上這孤兒，以錢相酬。孤兒一次次送食，漸積『千錢、千頭卷牙公豬、千頭豬』，自己也一級級買進高位。沃武特死時留下遺命：待孤兒前來哭喪，須把自己的妻子贈予他，以為紀念。

sensitivity.note: Recorded only in Codrington's summary of a native Mota manuscript too long to print; flagged as condensed.

passages.text: One of two more Stories from Mota in native manuscript, too long for insertion in full: the Story of Wowut-ta-Taragariga, whom his parents kept in the house till he was grown up, and then advanced to the highest Suqe rank. Another man of the same island taking the same step sent a portion of his feast to Wowut-ta-Taragariga by an orphan, all others being afraid of approaching the gamal of so high a rank. Wowut takes a liking to the orphan, and pays him with money. He goes again and again with food till he has 'thousands of money, thousands of boars, thousands of pigs with curled tusks,' and with these advances himself to high Suqe rank. Then Wowut dies, and directs that when his friend comes to mourn over him he is to be given his wife in memory of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.

title.en: Qat-wurunga, the Scurfy-Headed Boy, and Wetopunpun
title.zh: 結痂頭的卡特吳魯加與維托蓬蓬

region.en: Vanua Lava and Qakea, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島與烏阿凱阿（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded (native MS, summarized) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX note

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX, concluding note on two Mota stories

summary.en: Qat-wurunga was born of a mother killed by a fall from a tree and grew up in the forest; his uncle found him, took him home, and his uncle's wives, neglecting and ill-using him, named him Scurfy-head. Carried back to the midst of Vanua Lava, he snared birds; fat dripping through the fire called up Wetopunpun from under the earth — his dead father's ghost. With the charm 'Soso-punpun' the boy made food, gardens, a village, a gamal, pigs, fowls, a drum — all native wealth — and ate his way up the Suqe. Beguiled aboard a canoe from Maewo, he was carried off to be killed and eaten; one of the party took pity and loosed him, and the two paddled back to find all disappeared. His father Wetopunpun sat grieving on the beach till the Qakea people took him to their famine-struck island, where his charm filled gardens with food. Envied, he left them, and sits by Ro Som with all his possessions; a stone there representing him is a place of sacrifice to this day.
summary.zh: 卡特吳魯加的母親從樹上跌落而死，他遂生於林間、長於林間。母舅尋得他帶回家；舅母們冷淡苛待，給他起名『結痂頭』。他求舅舅把他送回森林深處——瓦努阿瓦島腹地，遠離海面。他張網捕鳥；一日烤鳥的油脂滴落火中、滲入地下，喚出地下的維托蓬蓬——那是他亡父之魂。男孩以咒語『Soso-punpun』憑空造出食物、園圃、村莊、會所、豬、雞、鼓——一切土著財富。舅父代他買盡蘇蓋各級；舅母們起初不信，赴宴一見其盛況，竟要留下做他的妻子，甚至要他剖胸取肝來吃。一艘馬埃沃來的獨木舟見其豬頜成堆，驚羨之下誘他睡去，把他運回本島要殺而食之；同行一人憐而鬆綁放他，二人划舟返回瓦努阿瓦，一切已消失無蹤。他被擄時其父維托蓬蓬每日坐在灘頭悲悼；烏阿凱阿人見之，渡海接他回島——那裡正逢饑荒，他以咒語變出滿園食物。眾人嫉妒，他便離去，攜全部財產坐到羅松身旁；那裡有一塊代表他的石頭，至今為獻祭之所。

sensitivity.note: Recorded only in Codrington's summary of a native Mota manuscript too long to print; flagged as condensed.

passages.text: The other of the two Mota stories too long for insertion in full: the Story of Qat-wurunga, who was born of a mother who had been killed by a fall from a tree, and grew up in the forest like the children in the Story of Taso. His maternal uncle finds him and takes him home, where his uncle's wives neglect him and ill-use him, and give him his name of Scurfy-head. The boy begs his uncle to take him back to the forest, and he carries him out of the sight of the sea into the midst of the island, Vanua Lava. Then he settles himself, and after a while snares birds. One day the fat of a bird roasting over the fire fell through on to the head of Wetopunpun beneath the earth, and he comes up above ground. This is the boy's father, the ghost of his dead father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.

passages.text: With the charm 'Soso-punpun, soso-punpun' — like the Kerembaembae of Story No. 1 — he makes food, gardens, a village, a gamal, pigs, fowls, a drum — all native wealth. Qat-wurunga's uncle comes to see him, and undertakes his advance to the highest ranks of the suqe, receiving his due payment of pigs. His wives, incredulous at first, go to a kolekole and see the youth they have despised in all his splendour. They desire to stay as his wives, and make him cut open his breast and give them some of his liver to eat. A canoe from Maewo comes over, and they find the fresh emblems of his rank; they challenge comparison with their own, and see open-mouthed with astonishment the number of jawbones of the pigs he has killed in his feasts. They beguile him to sleep, and carry him off to their own island to kill and eat him. While they are making preparations for their dance and feast, one of their party takes pity on him, unties and delivers him; the two paddle back to Vanua Lava. But when they reach Qat-wurunga's place all has disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.

passages.text: When he was captured his father Wetopunpun had gone to the beach and sat there grieving. The Qakea people, seeing him there day after day, paddled over and took him to their place, where there was a famine. There with his charm 'Soso-punpun' he makes gardens full of food appear. They envy him and he leaves them, and seeks a solitary place, where he sits down by the side of Ro Som with all his possessions round him. A stone there representing him is a place of sacrifice to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.
